decisions.title: How do we spell a whole-graph effect prohibition?
decisions.gist: Should a function be able to forbid an effect across its entire reachable call graph, and how is that written?
decisions.explainer: D-EFF1 (the effect-propagation engine) is ratified and positive effects like #(Net) already flow up the call graph. A prohibition is that same walk run inverted; this decides whether to ship it and how it reads.
decisions.story: A security engineer ships a payment-signing routine that must never touch the network. She wants to read one annotation at the root and trust that no callee, however deep, opens a socket. Auditing the whole tree by hand on every change is exactly what she is trying to stop doing.

options.name: Per-effect prohibition #(no_net)
options.detail: A prohibition annotation names one effect the function and its whole reachable graph may not use. It is the exact inverse of the positive set and runs on the ratified propagation engine, so it costs no new machinery. Cleanest when the rule is 'this one capability, never here'.

options.name: Sealed allowlist #(only Io)
options.detail: Instead of forbidding one effect, declare the complete set the function may use; everything outside it is forbidden. Stronger guarantee (closes the door on all nine other effects at once) but you must restate the full whitelist, and it reads oddly when you only meant to ban one thing.

options.name: Reuse the empty set #()
options.detail: #() already means 'no effects at all'. Lean on it: if you want no network, write a pure function. But #() forbids all ten effects, so it cannot express 'no Net while Io stays fine' -- it is all-or-nothing, which fails the security engineer who still needs to log.
options.code:
#() fn pure_sign(o: Order) -> Receipt { return seal(o) }
// forbids ALL effects -- you cannot say 'no Net but Io is OK'

comparisons.note: Effect rows list exactly the effects a function may use; absence means forbidden, and total functions <> forbid all effects. Closed rows give the allowlist (option B) for free.
comparisons.code: fun total-add( x : int, y : int ) : <> int { x + y }   // <> = no effects allowed

comparisons.note: No native effect prohibition; the ecosystem fakes it with a deny-lint at the crate root. Borrow the `forbid` spelling precedent; note it is lint-level, not type-level.
comparisons.code: #![forbid(unsafe_code)]   // any unsafe anywhere in the crate is a hard error

comparisons.note: Abilities are tracked in the type; calling an ability not granted in scope is a type error -- a positive set whose complement is the prohibition.
comparisons.code: step : '{IO} Nat -> Nat   -- only IO is reachable; anything else won't typecheck

decisions.title: Does temporal ordering get its own surface, or fall out of typestate?
decisions.gist: Does enforcing the legal ORDER of a value's states need a separate state-machine surface, or does it already emerge from typestate transition edges?
decisions.explainer: D-STATE1 / D-STATE-DECL is ratified: states live in a `state` block and methods carry #Transition(A -> B) / #State(C), erased in codegen. The open question is whether ordering across many states needs its own surface or is already pinned by the transition edges.
decisions.story: A hotel-booking dev models a Reservation that is Pending before payment, Confirmed after, and only then CheckedIn. He wants check_in on a still-pending reservation to be a compile error, and he wants the legal order -- pay before check-in -- enforced too, not just the single current state.

options.name: Pure typestate -- edges ARE the machine
options.detail: Each method's #Transition / #State annotation is one edge of the state machine; the legal order emerges because the only path to a late state runs through the earlier ones. No new surface. The order is implicit, so a reader reconstructs it by scanning the methods rather than reading it in one place.

options.name: Explicit transition block
options.detail: List the legal edges once inside the state declaration; every method must match a declared edge or it is rejected. The machine is readable in one place and methods are checked against it, at the cost of stating each edge twice (once in the block, once on the method).

options.name: Typestate + a #timeline phase block
options.detail: Keep per-method transitions, and add a #timeline naming the ordered happy path for documentation and exhaustiveness checking. Best self-documenting surface; but it introduces a second place to keep in sync and risks drifting from the actual edges.

comparisons.note: Typestate via phantom type params: each state is a distinct type, methods consume self and return the next-state type. Ordering emerges purely from which methods exist -- the model behind option A.
comparisons.code: impl Door<Open> { fn close(self) -> Door<Closed> { Door { _s: PhantomData } } }

comparisons.note: A dedicated typestate language: states are declared first-class and transitions named explicitly on operations -- the precedent for spelling the machine out (option B).
comparisons.code: state OpenFile case of File { method CloseFile()[>>ClosedFile]; }

comparisons.note: Protocols encoded with an indexed state monad; the legal order lives in the type index, statically enforced. Powerful but heavy -- the ordering is in the types, not a separate block.
comparisons.code: check_in : ST m () [res ::: Reservation Confirmed :-> Reservation CheckedIn]

decisions.title: What surface declares a protocol, and what gets generated?
decisions.gist: How does a user declare a request/response protocol so the compiler generates ordered client and server stubs that reject out-of-order messages?
decisions.explainer: D-LIN1 (single-use/linear values) and D-STATE1 (typestate) are both ratified -- the two pieces session types need: a handle used exactly once per step, threaded through states. This decides only the declaration surface and what the compiler emits.
decisions.story: A network-protocol implementer writes a handshake -- client sends Hello, server replies Ack, then client sends Data, server replies Done -- once, as a type. She wants both a client handle and a server handle generated, and she wants code that sends a message out of turn rejected at compile time, not at runtime on a customer's machine.

options.name: A `protocol` block, compiler generates both handles
options.detail: Write the ordered exchange once; the compiler generates Handshake.Client and Handshake.Server handle types, each step consuming and returning the handle (linear + typestate underneath). One declaration, both sides, out-of-order sends caught at compile time. The clearest beginner surface.

options.name: Hand-written linear+typestate handle (no new keyword)
options.detail: No new syntax: the user writes a #SingleUse handle and annotates each method with #Transition by hand; the session-ness is derived from the ratified pieces. Maximum reuse, zero new surface -- but the user writes both client and server by hand and keeps them dual, which is the boilerplate a protocol declaration exists to erase.

options.name: Protocol-as-data, generated at comptime
options.detail: Describe the protocol as an ordinary value and have comptime read it to emit both handles. Maximally programmable (protocols can be built from data) but the exchange is no longer readable as a sequence -- it is a struct literal, which buries the one thing a reader wants to see.

comparisons.note: The session_types crate encodes protocols as nested type constructors and computes the dual by trait -- correct but unreadable type soup, and no generation. Borrow the duality idea, avoid the spelling.
comparisons.code: type Server = Recv<Hello, Send<Ack, Recv<Data, Send<Done, Eps>>>>;

comparisons.note: lchannels derives session types from a protocol description and generates a case class per state -- the closest prior art to option A's generate-both-sides approach.
comparisons.code: case class Hello(cont: Out[Ack]); case class Ack(cont: In[Data])

comparisons.note: First-class session types built into the language as a sequence of typed sends/receives. The academic reference; the operator spelling is cryptic, so keep the ordering readable.

decisions.title: Does a type-position marker go before or after the type?
decisions.gist: When a plain value-tag like #Tainted decorates a type in a signature, does it sit before the type (#Tainted String) or after (String #Tainted)?
decisions.explainer: No gate clears this -- it is pure surface consistency, decidable today. Every other Jet marker is prefix (#Test fn, #Pure fn, #Unsafe block, #SingleUse struct); the only question is whether type-position tags match that or read better postfix.
decisions.story: A web dev marks form input #Tainted at the source and must write the type of a tainted string in a function signature. She needs one consistent spelling for #Tainted, #SingleUse, #NoCopy, and typestate markers -- the plain value-tags that decorate an existing type rather than minting a new one.

options.name: Prefix -- #Tainted String
options.detail: The tag comes before the type, matching every existing Jet marker (#Pure fn, #Test fn, #Unsafe, #SingleUse struct). One mental rule for all markers, wherever they appear. Reads as 'a tainted String'.

options.name: Postfix -- String #Tainted
options.detail: The tag follows the type, reading left-to-right as 'a String, tainted', like a refinement narrowing a base type. Arguably natural for qualifiers -- but it points the opposite way from every other #Marker in the language, so the reader now has two rules for where a marker lives.

comparisons.note: Outer attributes are prefix (#[test] fn foo). Jet's #Marker idiom already mirrors this; staying prefix keeps one rule.
`const` may sit before OR after the type (const char* vs char* const), and allowing both spawned decades of reader confusion. The cautionary tale: pick one position.
comparisons.code:
const char *a;   /* pointer to const */
char * const b;  /* const pointer */

comparisons.note: Taint is a runtime flag (-T mode), not a type spelling -- shows the concept's value but offers no placement to copy; Jet makes it static and must choose a position.

decisions.title: Do dynamic Data trees get fluent accessors, and how far?
decisions.gist: Should reading an untyped Data/Json tree get fluent accessors that compose with `?`, or stay pattern-match-only?
decisions.explainer: No gate -- Data and its variants (.Null/.Bool/.Int/.Float/.Text/.Array/.Object) shipped with D-ENC-DYN1. This decides whether to add an accessor layer over the tree and how far it reaches.
decisions.story: A dev consumes a third-party JSON blob with no fixed schema, so the #[Codable] derive doesn't fit. Today he pattern-matches the Data tree by hand. He wants to pull config.server.port as an Int without a five-level nested match that buries the one field he came for.

options.name: Pattern-match only (status quo floor)
options.detail: Keep the shipped mechanism: walk the tree with value-dispatch and pull each level out by hand. Nothing new to learn or maintain, and it is fully general -- but reaching one deep field costs a tower of nested matches, which is exactly the friction the user is complaining about.

options.name: Pattern-match + minimal fluent accessors
options.detail: Keep pattern-match as the floor and add a small accessor set -- .field(name), .at(i), and the leaf coercions .int()/.text()/.bool()/.float() -- each returning a Result so `?` chains cleanly. Covers the common 'reach a field, read a scalar' path in one line; missing key or wrong variant is a normal err.

options.name: Full jq-like path query
options.detail: Add a path mini-language so a whole route is one string. Most powerful for ad-hoc digging, but it is a second grammar to learn and test -- a query DSL living inside string literals -- which collides with I8's one-canonical-way bar.
options.code:
cfg.query("server.port").int()?        // a path language inside a string
cfg.query("items[0].name").text()?     // a whole second grammar to learn

comparisons.note: serde_json::Value: indexing returns a Value and typed getters return Option (as_i64). Borrow the typed-getter idea; Jet returns Result so `?` composes instead of Option.
encoding/json decodes to map[string]interface{}, forcing type assertions that panic on a wrong guess -- verbose and unsafe. The anti-pattern to avoid.
A full path-query language: powerful but an entire second grammar -- precisely what option C would import and what I8 rejects.

decisions.title: How does a function opt into deterministic replay?
decisions.gist: How does a user opt a function into deterministic replay, and what does the compiler guarantee about hidden non-determinism?
decisions.explainer: D-EFF1 is ratified and already tags the non-deterministic effects (#(Time), #(Rand), #(Net), #(Io)). This decides only the surface; the record/replay runtime harness is separate post-v1 build work, not decided here.
decisions.story: A game dev records a match's inputs and replays them to reproduce a one-in-a-thousand desync bug. He needs the compiler to guarantee that during replay nothing reads the clock, RNG, or network behind his back -- every non-deterministic source must be routed through something the replay harness can mock.

options.name: #Replayable marker (compile-time guarantee)
options.detail: A function marker rejects any reachable #(Time/Rand/Net/Io) that is not routed through a mockable capability -- the same inverse-propagation walk as D-PROP1. The compiler proves replay-soundness statically; the harness later swaps the capabilities. The guarantee lives in the type, so it cannot silently rot.
options.code:
#Replayable fn step(w: ^World, i: Input, clk: Clock) -> World { ... }
// any hidden clock.now() / rng in the reachable graph -> E0180 with the path

options.name: Library API over capability handles (no new syntax)
options.detail: No marker: the replay harness is just a library that passes mock capability handles, and the user routes non-determinism through them by convention. Zero new surface -- but nothing forces completeness, so one forgotten direct clock.now() silently breaks replay with no compile error.

options.name: Both -- marker for the proof, library for the harness
options.detail: Ship the #Replayable marker for the static guarantee AND the record/replay library for the runtime. The marker proves no hidden non-determinism; the library captures and plays back. Most complete story, and the two halves are naturally separable (the library is post-v1).

comparisons.note: Non-determinism is an effect you handle; a replay handler reinterprets rand/clock operations -- the model option A leans on, lifted to a marker over Jet's effect tags.
comparisons.code:
with handler { fun rand() { resume(replayed-value()) } }
fun () { simulate() }

comparisons.note: No language support; crates inject determinism by hand via trait objects and seeded RNG -- option B's manual capability passing, with no static completeness guarantee.
comparisons.code: fn step(w: &mut World, clk: &dyn Clock, rng: &mut StdRng) { /* ... */ }

comparisons.note: The record-replay debugger replays at the OS/runtime layer, orthogonal to the type system -- it is the harness half, showing the runtime piece is cleanly separable (post-v1).
comparisons.code: rr record ./game && rr replay   # deterministic playback, no source changes

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in tools/Tower/docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. questions.text: For generics, we use <T> -> can we use that?
questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: Can we keep it consistent, like to have json, toml, yaml, and csv all share the same data value?
questions.answer: Yes — and it's the recommended path. The D-ENC-DYN1 card now has Option A+ (one shared `Data` value for ALL four formats: json, toml, yaml, csv) as the recommendation. The internal `DataTree` is already the one universal model every format encodes/decodes through (that IS the serde architecture), so A+ just exposes it as the single dynamic value every `parse` returns. One vocabulary, one walker, no lossy surface. The only real cost: `json.parse` today returns the shipped `JSON` enum — A+ replaces it with `Data` as a clean break (no alias), migrating ~4 examples + the enum rename; cheapest done now, pre-1.0 (same spirit as core.json→core.encoding). Pick A+ on the ballot to lock it; there's a follow-up naming Owner Q (`Data` vs `Value`/`Doc`/`Node`, rec `Data`).

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.

questions.text: This seems to use outdated syntax. Please update based on the latest syntax & ensure there are examples of the best in class handling for this
questions.answer: Done — the card was written before several recent ratifications, so the syntax had drifted. Brought every line to current ratified syntax: (1) marker sigil @ -> # in derive-bracket form, so a user derive reads #[Wire] exactly like the built-in #[Codable] (D-ATTR1 reversed @->#; D-ATTR2 bracket form for trait-attaching markers); (2) dotless struct literal Packet{...} -> Packet.{ ... } (D-DOTCTOR2=A); (3) Bytes / b"hi" (neither exists) -> [U8] + byte-array literal [0x68,0x69], matching embed_bytes/sized-int examples; (4) splices made bare-identifier $name via local bindings ($fname/$tn) to respect the ratified D-CTMARKER1=C grammar (no $f.name expression-splice to invent); (5) buf: Buffer -> buf: edit Buffer (D-CAP3 capability-on-type, since the encoder mutates the buffer); sibling card D-METAREFLECT1 brought to the same sigil (#[Row]/#[Skip], has_marker("Skip")). Best-in-class examples: the 'Other languages' block now shows the two canonical author-side derive systems in full — Rust proc-macro derive returning a quote! TokenStream the compiler re-parses, and Swift @attached(extension) macros returning SwiftSyntax source the compiler re-checks — and notes both emit re-checked SOURCE (never a pre-validated tree), which is precisely the recommended Option A and why errors pin at the user's tag. Added Owner Q1 flagging the one genuinely-open sub-spelling (emit-template quoting: reuse "..."/"""...""" with {}-interpolation off inside emit, vs a distinct code-quote). Rec stays A. Decision stays open and pickable.
